result.summary: Pausanias describes the road from Daulis toward Delphi, the Phocicum assembly hall and the Cross-roads where Œdipus killed Laius. He then recounts varying traditions about the Delphic oracle's founders and the successive temples of Apollo.

scenes.title: Daulis road and the Phocicum
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the ascent of Parnassus from Daulis and the Phocian assembly hall with its statues of Zeus, Athene and Hera.

scenes.title: The Cross-roads of Œdipus
scenes.summary: At the meeting of three roads Œdipus killed his father; Laius and his attendant are buried there by Damasistratus.
scenes.stakes: Œdipus is fated to suffer woes after killing his father.

scenes.title: Who first held the oracle
scenes.summary: Pausanias reports traditions that the oracle belonged to Earth, then Poseidon, Themis and Apollo, and about its first prophets.

scenes.title: The five temples of Apollo
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the temples at Delphi: laurel, wax and wings, brass, stone, and the present one, doubting some legends.

notable_quotes.reason: Bœo's claim that Olen was first prophet and first to versify oracles.

analysis.text: Pausanias weighs competing local traditions and rejects those he finds implausible, showing his critical method.
The succession of temples and oracle owners reflects Delphi's prestige and how Greeks explained its origins, including links to the Hyperboreans.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias dates the fourth temple's burning by the Athenian archon and the Olympic victor, about 548 BC.

language_notes.text: Phocicum is the Phocians' common council hall, named from Phocis, the region whose towns sent delegates to it.
Oedipus's name, 'swollen foot', comes from this piercing; the infant was exposed because of a prophecy that he would kill his father.
'Polluted' means ritually defiled by bloodshed, especially the killing of a kinsman.
Refers to Oedipus's unwitting marriage to his mother Jocasta, and to his son Eteocles's wrongdoing in the quarrel with Polynices over the throne of Thebes.
'Unhewn stones' are rough, uncut stones piled up as a simple grave marker.
The Eumolpia is a lost epic poem about Eumolpus, founder of the Eleusinian Mysteries; it was attributed to Musæus, a legendary early poet.
"Meeting with the oracle" means coming upon the chasm by chance; the vapour was said to rise from a cleft in the ground.
Hexameters are lines of six metrical feet, the standard verse form of epic poetry and of Delphic oracles.
The Hyperboreans were a legendary people living far to the north, said to be especially beloved by Apollo.
Tempe is a valley in Thessaly; Apollo was said to have been purified there, and laurel from it was used in Delphic ritual.
The Hyperboreans were a legendary people dwelling far north, beyond the north wind, and were favoured by Apollo.
Pausanias derives the name from Pteras (Greek pteron, wing); adding a letter, Apteræi, a Cretan city, is said to be named similarly.
Acrisius, king of Argos, shut his daughter Danaë in a bronze chamber, yet Jove reached her as a shower of gold.
Hephæstus is the divine smith, so a bronze temple by him is a legend Pausanias rejects.
Charmers translates the Greek Keledones, enchanting singers; here they are golden figures, perhaps statues, singing above the pediment.
Dating is by the Athenian archon and Olympic victor, the Greek way of naming years; this corresponds to about 548 BC.

context_notes.text: Zeus, Athene and Hera were major Greek gods; placing them in the assembly hall put the Phocian meetings under divine protection.
Damasistratus, king of Plataea, is said to have given the unburied Laius and his attendant proper burial.
Themis is a goddess of divine law and order. Calauria was a small island off Trœzen in the Argolid, sacred to Poseidon.
Aguieus is a title of Apollo as guardian of streets and roads; here it is also the name of a Hyperborean.
The Lacedæmonians are the Spartans; their bronze-housed Athene Chalciœcus temple stood on the Spartan acropolis.
Trophonius and Agamedes were legendary architect brothers, said to have built Apollo's stone temple at Delphi.
The Amphictyones were the league of neighbouring peoples that administered Delphi's sanctuary.

literary_notes.text: This brief remark frames Oedipus's story as predestined, echoing the tragic theme that his doom could not be avoided.
The crossroads, where three roads meet, marks the point where Oedipus's life turns to disaster, and the stone-heaped graves make it a lasting monument to that moment.
Pausanias frames himself as a careful collector of competing traditions, signalling that he reports rather than endorses any single account.
The closing remark quietly undercuts Bœo's claim that a man, Olen, came first, reasserting the tradition of female prophets.
Pausanias' dry rationalizing comment shows his narrative voice: he sets legend beside practical reasoning rather than simply repeating it.
The first-person rejection shows the author weighing sources and judging myth critically.
Linking Pindar's golden singers to Homer's Sirens offers a literary explanation for a myth, treating it as poetic invention.
